title: Who is in your room
desc: Emerging and Progressing are not labels, they are predictions. What a level-one, a level-two and a level-three student can already do in your class, and the one habit that helps all of them.

cues.text: Welcome to Every Teacher, the podcast from EL Publishing. I'm Marcus. I teach ninth-grade biology, and three years ago a student walked into my second period who did not speak a word of English. I had no idea what to do. I'm here with Elena, who is the EL specialist in our building, and who basically saved that year for me.
That's generous. You saved it. I just showed up with a list.

You showed up with a list. So this series is that list. Six short episodes for the teacher who teaches content, not English, and has English learners in the room. Today, episode one: who is actually in your room. Because I think most of us get a roster with the letters E L next to a name, and a number, and that's it.

Right. And the number matters more than the letters. In Mississippi the English test is the E L P T, which is the ELPA twenty-one test. It gives a level from one to five in each of four domains: listening, speaking, reading and writing. And then a student is called Emerging, Progressing, or Proficient. Emerging is roughly levels one and two. Progressing is roughly three and four. Proficient is five, and that's when a student exits.
So when I see Emerging on my roster, what does that student actually do in a biology class?

Let's split it. A level one has usually been in the country for a few months or less. They can follow a routine they've seen before. They can point, match, sort, copy, and say a single word or a memorized phrase. What they can't do yet is follow you talking at normal speed for ten minutes, or read a paragraph of a textbook. And here's the important thing: that's not a learning problem. That's a language problem, and it's temporary.
That was my first mistake, honestly. I thought the student couldn't do biology. He could do biology. He'd done biology, in Spanish, in a pretty good school.

That's incredibly common. A newcomer often knows the content better than you'd guess. They know what a cell is. They just don't know the word cell. And a lot of the time, the word they know is a cognate. Célula. Cell. Fotosíntesis. Photosynthesis. Half of your academic vocabulary is sitting right there in Spanish already.
Okay, so that's level one. What's a level two?

A level two can handle short, familiar sentences. They can answer a yes or no question, or a question with a choice in it. Is this a plant cell or an animal cell. They can write a sentence if you give them the frame. They still need visuals, they still need you to slow down, and they still get lost when the lesson turns into fifteen minutes of talking.
And Progressing? Three and four?

This is the student most teachers underestimate in the other direction. A level three or four sounds fluent in the hallway. They joke, they argue, they've got the social English down. So teachers assume the academic English is there too. It usually isn't yet. They can read a grade-level text with support, they can write a paragraph, they can explain their thinking out loud, but the dense stuff, the textbook passage with four clauses in one sentence, the word problem where the question is buried in the middle, that's where they stall. And because they sound fluent, nobody notices.

That one hits home. I had a student I was sure was just not trying. Her writing was two sentences. Turned out she could tell me the entire process of mitosis if I let her talk, and she just couldn't get it onto paper yet.

That's a level three. Speaking ahead of writing. Very typical. And this is why the domains matter. Pull up the four scores, not just the overall. A student with a reading of four and a writing of two needs a different thing from you than a student with the reverse.
Where do I find the four scores?

Ask the EL teacher, or the counselor. In a lot of districts it's in the student information system. And if there's a Language Service Plan, an L S P, the scores are on page one. You're actually supposed to have a copy of that plan. It lists the accommodations you're expected to provide. If nobody has given it to you, ask. That's not being pushy. That's compliance.
Okay. So I know my levels. What's the one thing I do with that tomorrow?

One habit, for every level. Every single day, every student gets English in and English out. In means they understand something: you said it, they got it, because there was a picture, a gesture, a cognate, a model. Out means they produce something: a word, a sentence, a label on a diagram, a sentence in a pair. The level decides how big the in and the out are. For a level one the out might be one word. For a level four it's a paragraph. But nobody sits for ninety minutes and produces nothing.
In and out every day. That's doable.
It's doable. And it's the whole game. Everything else in this series is just ways to make the in understandable and the out possible.
Before we go, give me the thing to stop worrying about.

Stop worrying that you have to teach English. You don't. You teach biology. Your job is to teach biology in a way a learner of English can get into. The EL teacher handles grammar. You handle the language of biology: the words, the sentence shapes that biology uses, the way a lab report is organized. That's your lane, and it's a lane you're already an expert in.

That's episode one. Next time: how to make your lesson understandable without watering it down. Every Teacher is from EL Publishing. Everything we mention is free at radan55 dot github dot io slash everyteacher. Thanks for listening.
